qc.label_under_test: A label handed back between two people: one person labels another (sees him as a tyrant, calls him a bore, considers him reckless) and then that other person labels the first in return (and he sees me as a slacker); it fires on the returned label's opening ('me', 'as', 'a', 'like'), friendly or hostile labels alike, with or without a sentence introducing the pair. A plain tit-for-tat with no label (I hate him and he hates me), a one-way label, or two people labelling the same third party stays quiet, and it is weak when the narrator is labelled first and answers back.

neighbours.label: A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the narrator: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me or us (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us', whoever does the labelling and whether or not the label is handed back. The same second clause aimed at him, her, you or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.
fire: The office was quiet that Monday. My boss sees Daniel as a genius, and she sees me as a nuisance.
Rain hammered the windows of the old farmhouse. Grandpa called my cousin a saint, and he called me a troublemaker.
The village had not changed in fifty years. They welcome the tourists as guests, but they treat us as outsiders.
It was the last week of summer camp. The counselors regarded Lily as a leader, and they regarded me as a follower.
The courtroom fell silent. The prosecutor painted him as a victim and painted me as the villain.
Snow had buried the road by noon. Mom thinks of my sister as the responsible one, and she thinks of me as a dreamer.
The new school year started badly. The teacher saw Marco as a star pupil and saw us as a lost cause.
Our band played its first gig in a smoky bar. The critics hailed the drummer as a prodigy, and they dismissed me as a hack.
quiet: The office was quiet that Monday. My boss sees Daniel as a genius, and she sees him as her successor too.
Rain hammered the windows of the old farmhouse. Grandpa called my cousin a saint, and he called her a blessing.
The village had not changed in fifty years. They welcome the tourists as guests, but they treat them as wallets.
It was the last week of summer camp. The counselors regarded me as a follower.
The courtroom fell silent. The prosecutor painted me as the villain, and I called him a liar.
Snow had buried the road by noon. Mom thinks of my sister as the responsible one, and she thinks of you as a dreamer.
The new school year started badly. The teacher praised Marco and ignored the rest of us completely.
Our band played its first gig in a smoky bar. The critics hailed the drummer as a prodigy, and they loved the singer as well.

predictions: Most fire sentences over 0.30; near misses with him/her/them/you under 0.30. Written blind from the label by a second author (label-only).
